newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan factions still far from negotiating table.
newsitem.headline: Afghan factions still far from negotiating table.

text.p: Afghanistan's warring parties are no closer to reaching the negotiating table despite the best efforts of both the Pakistan government and the United Nations.

Pakistan is trying to convince the factions to sign on to a political commission with members from all sides. Both the northern alliance and the Taleban have agreed in principle to the idea, but their pre-conditions may prove to be insurmountable.
While the politicians bicker, alternately raising and dashing hopes, the two sides are preparing for a major battle on the plains north of Kabul.
Pakistan's negotiator, Iftikar Murshed, returned from the Taleban headquarters in the southern city of Kandahar on Sunday.
"I have brought home extremely good news, my visit to Kandahar was a real success," Murshed is reported as saying on his return.
"(The Taleban) agreed to form a broad-based commission which should not only include the northern alliance, but also all other groups in Afghanistan," he said.
But senior Taleban officials said that there were conditions before talks could begin, most notably that the opposition should release Taleban prisoners.

There are no reliable figures on how many Taleban fighters the opposition holds, but large numbers were taken in May when the Taleban were surrounded -- and many of them killed -- when the opposition recaptured the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif.

Opposition spokesmen say that there can be no preconditions to the talks, and that the issue of the prisoners should be discussed by the commission along with other issues such as a ceasefire and long-term plans for bringing peace to Afghanistan.

The Taleban on Sunday accused the opposition of killing some prisoners and maltreating others. In a letter to the International Committee of the Red Cross the Taleban foreign minister complained that the opposition was not allowing Red Cross workers access to the prisoners.

The anti-Taleban alliance has demanded the demilitarisation of Kabul. The opposition north of Kabul -- led by Ahmed Shah Masood, the most important military commander in the former government ousted from the city by the Taleban last September -- says that if the Taleban do not withdraw from the city, they will be attacked.
The peace process is locked in an impasse with both sides more interested in exploring the military options, according to one analyst in Kabul.
"There is no problem to get them to agree in principal to any of the plans, but both sides have conditions and the conditions they lay down are almost without fail unacceptable to the other side.

"Both sides know this. The only conclusion that I can come to is that they want to be seen to be interested in a negotiated solution while they are putting most of their efforts into a military solution," said the analyst, who wished to remain anonymous.

Two weeks ago, the opposition advanced to within 12 miles (20 km) of Kabul. Since then there has been little significant change in the front line, but independent observers say that the opposition has been sending more men and supplies down to the battle zone.

A meeting between opposition leaders and the U.N. special envoy to Afghanistan scheduled for last Thursday was first postponed and then cancelled when the opposition representatives said that they could not make it to Mazar-i-Sharif.

The Taleban, who control two-thirds of Afghanistan, have vowed to take the whole country and rid it of the warlords whom they blame for the descent into chaos since the defeat of the communists five years ago.
There have been many attempts during that time to stop the fighting, including one agreement signed in the Ka'aba in Mecca, Islam's most holy site, but none has had any lasting results.
